fix(sso): allow clearing the SSO connection name (#13143)

* fix(sso): allow clearing the SSO connection name

The update flow silently dropped attempts to clear an SSO connection's
human-friendly name:

- The service dumped the patch with `exclude_none=True`, so an explicit
  `name: null` was removed from the update and never applied.
- The `name` field used `NonEmptyStr` (`min_length=1`), so `name: ""`
  failed validation with a 422.

Switch the update to `exclude_unset=True` so explicit nulls are preserved
(matching the PATCH convention used by other update services), and treat a
blank/whitespace-only `name` as `None` at the schema level so an empty
string clears the label too.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_0138Kq5PDRGxhuwLCzbErXPE

Replace the local blank-to-None validator with the existing
`EmptyStrToNone` type from `polar.kit.schemas`, matching the convention
used by the other schemas. Behaviour is unchanged: a blank or
whitespace-only `name` still normalizes to `null`.

subject: fix(checkout_link): normalize empty query params to None on redirect (#13241)
message:
fix(checkout_link): normalize empty query params to None on redirect (#13241)

* fix(checkout_link): normalize empty query params to None on redirect

The checkout-link redirect endpoint accepted its string query parameters
as plain `str | None`, so `?customer_email=` was parsed as an empty
string and prefilled onto the checkout. An empty `customer_email` then
slipped past the "required when no customer is attached" check (which
only tests `is None`), allowing a checkout to be confirmed and a Customer
to be created with an empty email.

Apply the existing `EmptyStrToNone` validator to every string query
parameter on the redirect endpoint so empty and whitespace-only values
are normalized to `None` at the edge, consistent with how the checkout
and customer schemas already treat these fields.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01Bg6KKarXSm9SJmd2rUXQcY

* fix(checkout_link): drop consumed prefill keys from redirect passthrough

The redirect endpoint re-appends unhandled query params to the checkout
URL, excluding known prefill keys via
`(k not in query_prefill or query_prefill[k] is None)`. The second branch
was effectively dead: a present string query param was always a string,
never None, so prefill keys were never forwarded.

Now that empty prefill values are normalized to None, that branch fires
for empty inputs (e.g. `?customer_email=`), re-appending the raw empty
string to the redirect URL instead of dropping it. Match on key presence
alone so consumed prefill keys are dropped regardless of value, while
genuine passthrough params are still forwarded.

subject: fix: send subscription renewal confirmation only after payment succeeds (#13268)
message:
fix: send subscription renewal confirmation only after payment succeeds (#13268)

* fix(order): send renewal confirmation on payment, not on order creation

Async subscription cycles create the order as pending and charge it in a
later task, so the confirmation email was enqueued before the charge was
attempted. A failed renewal then sent both "subscription renewed" and
"payment failed".

Move the single enqueue onto the paid transition in _on_order_paid.

* fix(order): emit the paid transition once for settled subscription orders

_create_order called _on_order_created after settling payment, so a sync
charge under the currency minimum — typical of a proration — ran the paid
transition twice: once from trigger_payment, once from the born-paid branch
of _on_order_created. That duplicated the confirmation email, the order.paid
webhook, the receipt allocation and the paid event.

Emit creation events before settling, and let each settling branch own its
own transition. order.created now consistently precedes order.paid across
all cycle paths.

* fix(email): make the past-due email a clear single failure notice

The past-due email buried the failure
  in billing jargon ("payment is past
  due"), so a customer could not tell what had happened or what to do. State
  plainly that the payment failed and give the access-loss notice an urgent
  treatment.
Keep the wording neutral: the same email also fires for trial-conversion
  charges, which are a first payment rather than a renewal.

* fix(order): emit order.updated when dunning starts without a payment method

order.created is now emitted before payment settles, so a cycle order that
immediately enters dunning reported no retry schedule and an active
subscription, with no later webhook to correct it.

* test(order): assert the paid transition fires exactly once

The confirmation-email assertions checked membership or tolerated repeats,
so a duplicate paid transition — and the duplicate receipt allocation and
order.paid webhook that come with it — passed unnoticed. Assert counts, spy
the transition itself, and cover the zero-due branch.

* Tweak email

subject: Fix order payment lock wedging forever, breaking dunning retries (#13272)
message:
Fix order payment lock wedging forever, breaking dunning retries (#13272)

* fix(order): don't dead-letter dunning retries on a held payment lock

A payment lock left behind by an unresolved PaymentIntent makes every
subsequent trigger raise PaymentAlreadyInProgress, which Dramatiq retries
hourly until the message dead-letters. Log and return instead, mirroring
void_pending_orders_for_subscription.

* feat(stripe): add PaymentIntent cancellation and per-order lookup

No cancellation support existed, and nothing could find an order's
intents without an id stored on our side.

* feat(stripe): release a stale payment lock on payment_intent.canceled

The event was unhandled entirely. Handle it so a confirmed cancellation
releases the lock and advances dunning as a failure would.

Only a stale lock is released: a fresh one belongs to an attempt still in
flight, and a cancellation arriving for an older intent of the same order
must not cut it short. The dunning interval index is clamped because a
cancelled attempt records no Payment, leaving the failure count at zero.

* feat(order): cancel the intents behind a stale payment lock on a schedule

Hourly, find orders holding a lock past the stale threshold and cancel
their pending PaymentIntents, located by searching Stripe on the order
metadata. Intents that are settling are left alone, as Stripe resolves
those on its own.

The lock is deliberately untouched here: a requires_action intent can
still settle to succeeded through Stripe's SCA recovery email, so
releasing before cancellation is confirmed would risk a double charge.

* fix(order): don't cancel a payment intent whose lock was refreshed since the scan

* refactor(order): move payment lock staleness check to Order model

* perf(order): drop eager loading from the stale payment lock worker

* feat(payment): record a Payment for intents that haven't charged yet

* refactor(order): cancel stale payment locks from the recorded payment

* fix(payment): mark the payment failed when its intent is canceled

* refactor(payment): record pending intents from webhooks

* fix(payment): correct the method and the dedup on recorded intents

subject: Fix/payment pending intent race (#13315)
message:
Fix/payment pending intent race (#13315)

* fix(payment): stop the pending intent recorder racing the charge

payment_intent.created fires at the same moment as charge.succeeded, so
both handlers found no row and both inserted: two payments for one
charge. Its payload also always carries a null latest_charge, so a late
delivery flipped a settled payment back to pending.

Order payments confirm at creation, so requires_action alone covers the
intents a payment lock can wedge on. Drop the created handler, refuse to
write over a row already re-keyed onto a charge or past pending, and take
the row lock so a charge webhook can't land between the read and the
write.

* chore(payment): repair payments damaged by the pending intent race

Soft-deletes the intent-keyed duplicates in batches, and reconciles
charge-keyed rows sitting at pending against Stripe. Dry-run by default.

subject: fix(payment): harden failed-intent upsert against concurrent-webhook race (#13325)
message:
fix(payment): harden failed-intent upsert against concurrent-webhook race (#13325)

upsert_from_stripe_payment_intent did a plain check-then-insert with no row
lock and no IntegrityError handling. When a payment_intent.payment_failed
webhook raced a sibling delivery (e.g. requires_action) for the same
PaymentIntent on another worker, both found no row and the pending duplicate
INSERT crashed with a unique violation on ix_payments_processor_id — surfacing
far from the bug via an unrelated autoflush.

Apply the same locking + savepoint fallback pattern already used by
upsert_pending_from_stripe_payment_intent (#13315): take a SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
lock via get_by_stripe_payment_intent_id, and wrap the insert in a SAVEPOINT
that falls back to re-fetching and updating the row that won the race on
IntegrityError.

fix(backoffice): handle Plain httpx timeouts in reply_in_plain (SERVER-4VY) (#13327)

The backoffice "Reply in Plain" flow calls plain.create_feedback_thread,
which issues several Plain GraphQL calls over an httpx.AsyncClient with a
10s/5s timeout. reply_in_plain only caught PlainServiceError, so a slow or
unresponsive Plain API surfaced raw httpx.ReadTimeout/ConnectTimeout as an
unhandled 500.

Catch httpx.RequestError (covers ReadTimeout/ConnectTimeout/TimeoutException
and other transport errors) alongside the existing PlainServiceError handling,
showing an error toast and redirecting back to the feedback page — matching the
pattern established in #13262.

subject: server/meter: chunk billing-entry customer prefetch to fix SQL timeouts (#13362)
message:
server/meter: chunk billing-entry customer prefetch to fix SQL timeouts (#13362)

* server/meter: chunk billing price prefetch to avoid SQL timeout

PR #13361 replaced N sequential per-customer price lookups with a single
upfront prefetch: it collected every distinct customer_id for the meter's
entire remaining backlog via `get_distinct_customer_ids` (an unbounded
`SELECT DISTINCT ... JOIN` with no limit), then one batched price lookup.
After an event-ingestion spike left large unprocessed backlogs, that
distinct-scan repeatedly hit the 30s statement timeout — the fix had traded
N small round trips for one query whose cost scaled with the whole backlog.

Bound the per-query cost instead: stream events in billing order and process
them in batches of `_BILLING_ENTRY_BATCH_SIZE` (500). Each batch collects its
own distinct customer_ids in Python (no extra SQL) and does one
`get_by_customers_and_meter` lookup, so query cost scales with the batch, not
the backlog. Business logic is unchanged — direct-over-seat priority, trial
skipping, watermark advancement, and `subscription.update_meters` enqueueing
all preserved. The per-customer race fallback is kept as a safety net.

`EventRepository.get_distinct_customer_ids` had no other callers and is
removed.

subject: server/meter: load billing watermark after row lock (#13369)
message:
server/meter: load billing watermark after row lock (#13369)

The billing actor previously eager-loaded last_billed_event with joinedload in the same SELECT FOR UPDATE statement. Under PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED, a waiter can receive the updated meter row while the joined event still comes from the pre-lock snapshot. That stale relationship makes the actor replay a full page and enqueue another continuation without advancing the watermark.

Use selectinload so SQLAlchemy locks and reads the fresh meter row first, then loads last_billed_event in a second statement after the lock is held. This keeps the keyset cursor coherent across concurrent billing continuations and stops no-progress re-enqueue loops.

Validated with uv run task lint, uv run task lint_types, uv run pytest tests/meter -q, and uv run pytest tests/event tests/subscription -q.

subject: fix(order): cap over-refunded tax on partial refunds with applied balance (#13381)
message:
fix(order): cap over-refunded tax on partial refunds with applied balance (#13381)

calculate_refunded_tax_from_subtotal derived tax by applying
tax_amount / net_amount to the whole refund_amount. When an order
collected debt (applied_balance_amount > 0), refundable_amount exceeds
net_amount, so a partial refund larger than net_amount applied the tax
ratio to the non-taxable applied-balance portion. This could return a
tax larger than the total tax collected, producing the impossible state
refunded_tax_amount > tax_amount and over-refunding tax to customers.

Cap the computed tax at refundable_tax_amount, matching the sibling
method calculate_refunded_tax_from_total, and short-circuit untaxed
orders to mirror that method and avoid a 0/0 division when net_amount
is 0.

subject: Fix session state after concurrent member creation race (#13380)
message:
Fix session state after concurrent member creation race (#13380)

* fix: prevent PendingRollbackError in member get-or-create race

`MemberService.get_or_create_by_email` and `create_owner_member` retried
after an `IntegrityError` from the partial unique index by re-querying on
the same session. A failed `flush()` leaves the session in an aborted
transaction state, so the follow-up query raised `PendingRollbackError`
and surfaced as a 500 (seen via `assign_seat` → `POST /v1/customer-seats`).

Wrap the create/flush in a `session.begin_nested()` savepoint and roll it
back before re-querying, matching the pattern already used in
`organization`, `github_repository_benefit`, and `event_type`. The
re-query now returns the concurrently-created member as intended.

Add regression tests for both methods that reproduce the poisoned-session
race and assert the existing member is returned without raising.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01UTjQv3Lpfh4g36cH7auZ84

* fix: release member-create savepoint on the success path

The savepoint added to fix the PendingRollbackError race was left open on
successful creation: `begin_nested()` was only rolled back in the
IntegrityError branch, never committed/released otherwise. SQLAlchemy keeps
that nested transaction active until the outer transaction commits, so
callers that create members in a loop within one session — notably the
organization owner-member backfill (`_backfill_owner_members`) — accumulated
unreleased savepoints/subtransactions.

Scope the flush with `async with session.begin_nested():` in both
`create_owner_member` and `get_or_create_by_email`. The context manager
releases the savepoint on success and rolls it back on IntegrityError,
matching the pattern already used in `transaction/service/dispute.py`.
Verified with `session.in_nested_transaction()`: previously True after each
successful call, now False.

fix(web): stop 403 spam from org billing queries for non-admin members (#13387)

`DashboardSidebar` called `useOrganizationSubscription` unconditionally, only
to decide whether to render the "Introducing Polar Plans" upsell card. The
endpoint is guarded by `AuthorizeOrgManageRead`, which enforces the
`organization:manage` policy, so a plain org member gets a 403 on every
dashboard page. `defaultRetry` only short-circuits on 401 and 404, so each
mount produced four console errors.

matching the existing pattern in `PlanUpsell`. Members no longer see the upsell
card, which is correct anyway since it links to a settings page they can't
reach.

Express the gate as an `enabled` parameter on `useOrganizationSubscription` and
`useOrganizationPlans` rather than passing `undefined` as the org id. This is
the dominant convention across the query hooks (`org.ts`, `events.ts`,
`metrics.ts`), keeps `undefined` meaning "no org yet" instead of also meaning
"not allowed", and keeps the query key stable so gating no longer churns the
cache. Replaces the `gatedOrgId` workaround in `PlanUpsell`.

The scheduler's main loop sleeps until the next scheduled job, and the
heartbeat was only refreshed after that sleep. When the next job was more
than HEARTBEAT_STALENESS_SECONDS away, a healthy but idle scheduler read
as stale, so the health check returned 503 and the instance was restarted.

Cap the idle sleep to HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL_SECONDS so the loop wakes and
refreshes the heartbeat well within the staleness window regardless of
job cadence.

perf(invariants): speed up slow invariant checks (#13436)

* perf(invariants): bound payout amount check to recent payouts

Aggregate paid transactions only for the recent payout set instead of
grouping over the entire transactions history, which was hitting the
statement timeout. Pure rewrite — the outer join already discarded
non-recent payouts, so results are unchanged.

* perf(invariants): add covering index for deleted-customer check

Add a partial covering index on customers(deleted_at, id) WHERE
deleted_at IS NOT NULL so the active-subscriptions-for-deleted-customers
invariant can scan deleted customers index-only, skipping the per-row
heap fetches that were driving the statement timeout on cold cache.

* fix(invariants): drop invalid leftover index before concurrent build

A canceled CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY leaves an INVALID index; since the
migration row isn't recorded until the build finishes, a rerun would fail
on the existing name. Drop it first to recover, matching the other
concurrent-index migrations.

subject: fix(tax): accept post-2023 Taiwanese unified business numbers (#13445)
message:
fix(tax): accept post-2023 Taiwanese unified business numbers (#13445)

Taiwan's Ministry of Finance relaxed the UBN check rule in April 2023:
the weighted digit sum only needs to be divisible by 5 instead of 10.
stdnum still implements the original rule, so roughly half of the UBN
issued since then were rejected at checkout with an invalid tax ID error
(e.g. 62140097).

Add a TWVATValidator that falls back to the relaxed checksum when stdnum
reports InvalidChecksum, keeping its length and format checks. Both the
original and the relaxed rule keep the seventh digit "7" alternative.

subject: feat(payment_method): remind customers before their card expires (#13424)
message:
feat(payment_method): remind customers before their card expires (#13424)

* feat(email): add payment method expiration reminder template

Adds the `payment_method_expiration_reminder` email: template component,
Pydantic props, and the generated TypeScript types.

The props carry the card (brand, last4, expiry) and the names of the
products it pays for, so the email can name what is at risk. Product
names are a list because one card can back several subscriptions; the
template pluralises accordingly.

Nothing sends this template yet.

* feat(payment_method): remind customers before their card expires

Mirrors the subscription renewal reminder: an hourly cron actor scans for
cards expiring within 30 days and fans out one job per card, which sends
the reminder via the customer's portal session.

Only cards backing a billable subscription are considered — an expiring
card with nothing to charge is not actionable — and the correlated EXISTS
on the indexed payment_method_id also keeps the scan narrow, since card
expiry lives in the untyped method_metadata JSONB with no index.

Deduplication is derived from email_logs rather than a new column, keyed
on the payment method and its expiry month/year. Matching on integers
rather than a formatted date avoids the string-format coupling the
renewal reminder carries, and including the expiry means Stripe's
card-updater webhook correctly re-arms the reminder for the new date.

Expiry months are computed in Python rather than with SQL date maths:
exp_month/exp_year are unvalidated JSONB, and make_date() on a bad value
would raise and take down the whole scan.

Organizations can opt out via customer_email_settings; the key is
read-defaulted to enabled so no data migration is needed.

* feat(web): add card expiration reminder email setting

Exposes the payment_method_expiration_reminder toggle in the
organization's customer email settings.

* refactor(email): use Array.at() for the last product name

Reads more clearly than indexing with length - 1.

* fix(payment_method): ignore soft-deleted subscriptions when scanning cards

The EXISTS predicate used a raw select() rather than the repository base
statement, so it missed the soft-deletion filter. A card whose only
billable subscription had been soft-deleted was selected and enqueued,
then dropped by the sender because the products lookup — which does
filter soft-deletions — came back empty.

* feat(payment_method): inherit cycle setting, remind ahead of month end

Addresses review feedback on #13424.

Default payment_method_expiration_reminder to the subscription_cycled
preference instead of enabling it for everyone. Organizations that turned
every customer email off shouldn't have a new one switched on silently.
The key is absent from settings written before this template existed, so
this resolves at read time via the existing lazy-materialization path —
no backfill needed. resolve_customer_email_settings() is the single place
that rule lives, shared by the API schema and the send path.

Shorten the reminder window from 30 to 20 days. Cards expire at the end of
their month, so a 30 day window always fired on the 1st, where the reminder
competes with everyone else's monthly billing mail. 20 days moves it to
around the 9th-12th, depending on month length.

subject: fix(customer): free external_id and emit customer.deleted when deleting with anonymize (#13453)
message:
fix(customer): free external_id and emit customer.deleted when deleting with anonymize (#13453)

* fix(customer): free external_id when deleting with anonymize

Deleting a customer with `anonymize=true` routes through
`CustomerService.anonymize()`, which sets `deleted_at` directly and
deliberately retains `external_id`. That bypasses
`CustomerRepository.soft_delete()`, the only place that clears the column.

Since the unique constraint on `(organization_id, external_id)` doesn't
account for `deleted_at`, the external ID stays locked forever. The
application-level conflict check filters out deleted customers, so the
collision only surfaces as an IntegrityError on insert, with no
self-serve way to release the value.

Clear the column in `anonymize()` too, keeping the original value in
`user_metadata.__external_id` — the same place `soft_delete()` stores it,
and what `Customer.saved_external_id` reads back. The legal/audit purpose
of retaining the external ID is preserved; it just no longer occupies the
unique slot. API and webhook payloads are unchanged, since the schema
already resolves `external_id` from `saved_external_id`.

Includes a batched backfill for customers already stuck in that state.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01L5MXyAUeYu5qfQ2YXU34AT

* refactor(customer): move external_id backfill to a script

Releasing the external IDs of already-deleted customers is maintenance
work on a busy table, not a schema change — it belongs with the other
backfills rather than in the migration chain.

Use `run_batched_update` from `scripts/helper.py`, which already handles
the batching loop, per-batch commits, inter-batch sleep, and progress
reporting, and accepts a session so the script is testable.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01L5MXyAUeYu5qfQ2YXU34AT

* fix(customer): emit customer.deleted when deleting with anonymize

`delete(anonymize=True)` returned the result of `anonymize()`, which set
`deleted_at` itself and never reached `soft_delete()` — the only place
that enqueues the `customer.deleted` webhook and system event. Deleting a
customer with anonymization therefore told integrators nothing beyond a
`customer.updated` event, leaving them unable to reconcile the deletion.

Make `anonymize()` scrub PII only and have `delete()` always funnel
through `soft_delete()`, so both paths emit the same deletion signals and
free the external ID through one code path.

This also fixes `delete(anonymize=True)` silently doing nothing when the
customer was already anonymized: `anonymize()` returns early in that case,
so the early return skipped the soft delete entirely.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01L5MXyAUeYu5qfQ2YXU34AT

* fix(customer): report the released external ID in customer events

The customer event tasks re-read the customer when the job runs, which is
after the request transaction commits. Deletion clears `external_id`, so
by then the column is null and every event reported
`customer_external_id: null` — including `customer.deleted`, the one event
an integrator needs to reconcile the deletion against its own records.

Read `saved_external_id` instead, which falls back to the value deletion
stored in metadata. For a live customer it returns the column verbatim, so
this only changes what deleted customers report.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01L5MXyAUeYu5qfQ2YXU34AT

* refactor(customer): free external_id only at the deletion boundary

Clearing `external_id` was duplicated: `soft_delete()` did it, and
`anonymize()` did it too — a leftover from when `anonymize()` was itself
the terminal deletion path. Now that `delete()` always funnels through
`soft_delete()`, the copy in `anonymize()` is not just redundant but
wrong: `anonymize()` no longer deletes, so calling it on its own would
release a live customer's external ID.

That failure would have been quiet. `saved_external_id` falls back to
metadata, so the API would keep reporting the external ID while
`get_by_external_id_and_organization`, which queries the column, stopped
finding the customer.

Leave `anonymize()` preserving `external_id` as it always did, and let
deletion free it. `delete(anonymize=True)` still recycles the external ID,
now through one code path instead of two.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01L5MXyAUeYu5qfQ2YXU34AT

* fix(customer): make a delete emit only customer.deleted

Delete first, then anonymize. Scrubbing PII is cleanup that follows the
deletion rather than a step before it, and running it on an already-deleted
customer keeps the write from being announced as an update.

That reordering alone wasn't enough: `CustomerRepository.update()` enqueued
`customer.updated` unconditionally, and a soft delete is an update —
`RepositorySoftDeletionMixin.soft_delete()` is implemented as
`self.update(update_dict={"deleted_at": ...})`. So both writes announced
themselves, and the anonymize path emitted two `customer.updated` webhooks
around the `customer.deleted` one.

Move that enqueue inside the existing `if not customer.deleted_at` guard,
which already suppressed the matching system event. Both delete paths now
emit exactly one webhook and one event, both `customer.deleted`.

Restoring a customer still emits `customer.updated`: the guard reads
`deleted_at` after the update is applied, so clearing it notifies as
before. Updating a customer that stays deleted is now silent, where it
previously sent a webhook with no accompanying event.

subject: perf(billing_entry): skip session sync in update_order_item_id (#13479)
message:
perf(billing_entry): skip session sync in update_order_item_id (#13479)

The batched UPDATE in update_order_item_id is ORM-enabled, so with no
synchronize_session set it defaults to "auto" -> "evaluate". That makes
SQLAlchemy walk the entire session identity map on every batch and, for
each resident BillingEntry, test its id against the batch's 1000-element
IN list (the evaluator compiles in_() to a linear `a in b` scan).

Per-batch cost is therefore proportional to the number of resident
entries, making the loop quadratic. On subscriptions with 200k+ entries
this is enough to blow the 600s job timeout.

Nothing reads order_item_id off these objects in-session afterwards, so
synchronization buys nothing here.

Measured with the added benchmarks (deselected by default, run with
-m benchmark):

  resident entries   before    after
             5,013    234 ms    31 ms
            10,013    387 ms    34 ms
            20,013    752 ms    32 ms
            40,013   1472 ms    34 ms

The 40k row reproduces the ~1.5s/batch seen in production.

subject: fix(billing_entry): filter deleted_at in link_pending UPDATEs (#13500)
message:
fix(billing_entry): filter deleted_at in link_pending UPDATEs (#13500)

The direct UPDATE WHERE statements in link_pending_by_subscription_and_price
and link_pending_by_subscription_and_meter build a raw update() and bypass
the repository's soft-deletion base statement, so they omitted the
`deleted_at IS NULL` predicate.

Two consequences:

- Performance: the only remaining composite index is
  ix_billing_entries_s_d_oi_pp (subscription_id, deleted_at, order_item_id,
  product_price_id). Without a predicate on deleted_at (column 2), Postgres
  can only bound the scan on subscription_id and reads every billing entry
  for the subscription, filtering order_item_id/product_price_id in the
  index instead of using them as bounds. On long-lived, high-volume
  subscriptions that scans the entire history instead of just the pending
  entries. Adding `deleted_at IS NULL` restores full index usage.

- Correctness: the compute path filters soft-deleted entries via
  get_base_statement(), but the link path did not, so a soft-deleted
  pending entry could be linked to a new order item it was excluded from.

Add `deleted_at IS NULL` to both UPDATEs and assert soft-deleted entries
stay unlinked in the existing tests.

subject: perf(billing_entry): count entries directly for count meters (#13505)
message:
perf(billing_entry): count entries directly for count meters (#13505)

* perf(billing_entry): count entries directly for count meters

`_get_metered_line_item` computed a count meter's quantity via
`COUNT(events.id)` over the `events → billing_entry` join. The planner
drives from `billing_entry` (the full pending set) and does one primary-key
probe into `events` per entry — ~11s for a 206k-entry subscription and worse
above that, timing out cycle order creation for high-volume metered subs.

There is exactly one billing entry per event (`from_metered_event`), and
entries are pre-filtered to the meter at creation, so for a count meter the
quantity is just the number of consumption entries. Count the entries
directly (`count_pending_entries`, no join) and subtract the few
system-event entries (`count_pending_system_entries`, index-driven on
org+customer+source) to reproduce the `source='user'` count. ~112ms vs ~11s.

Only count meters are affected; sum/max/avg/unique still read per-event
values and keep the existing events path.
